Art. 5(1)(a).o: People should not be surprised or harmed by what you do with their data.
Art. 5(1)(a).a: For each entry on the data map, write down the purpose and lawful basis, and make sure your privacy notice says the same thing.
Art. 5(1)(a).e: A regulator compares what you tell people with what you actually do.
Art. 5(1)(a).r: Data map with purposes; approved privacy notice.

Art. 5(1)(b).o: Data collected for one job should not quietly be reused for another.
Art. 5(1)(b).a: Check each data map entry has one clear purpose. Before reusing data for something new, check the new use fits, or ask again.
Art. 5(1)(b).e: They look for data reused for marketing or analytics without a check.
Art. 5(1)(b).r: Purposes on the data map; DPIA or note for any new use.

Art. 5(1)(c).o: Less data means less to lose and less to look after.
Art. 5(1)(c).a: Go through each form and system on the data map and remove fields you do not use.
Art. 5(1)(c).e: They ask why each piece of data is needed.
Art. 5(1)(c).r: Data categories on the data map; review notes.

Art. 5(1)(d).o: Wrong data can lead to wrong decisions about people.
Art. 5(1)(d).a: Make it easy for people to update their details, and correct errors when you find them.
Art. 5(1)(d).e: They check how corrections are made and how fast.
Art. 5(1)(d).r: Correction requests in the request tracker; procedure.

Art. 5(1)(e).o: Old data is a risk with no benefit.
Art. 5(1)(e).a: Set a retention period for each data map entry, and delete or anonymise data when it ends.
Art. 5(1)(e).e: They ask for your retention schedule and proof that deletion happens.
Art. 5(1)(e).r: Retention periods on the data map; deletion logs.

Art. 5(2).o: It is not enough to comply. You must be able to prove it.
Art. 5(2).a: Keep the records in this product up to date and export the accountability report when asked.
Art. 5(2).e: This is the first thing a regulator asks for.

Art. 6.o: There are six lawful bases. Every use of data needs one of them.
Art. 6.a: Pick one lawful basis for each data map entry. If you pick legitimate interests, write down why your interest is not outweighed by the person's.
Art. 6.e: They check every activity has a basis and that it fits.
Art. 6.r: Lawful basis on each data map entry; legitimate interest assessments.

Art. 7.o: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, clear, and as easy to withdraw as to give.
Art. 7.a: For every place you ask for consent, record the wording, how it is collected, where the proof is kept, and how people withdraw.
Art. 7.e: They ask you to prove a specific person consented.
Art. 7.r: Consent records with wording and screenshots.

Art. 8.o: Children need a parent's consent for online services below the national age (13 to 16).
Art. 8.a: If you offer online services to children, check the age and get parental consent where needed.
Art. 8.e: They look at age checks and parental consent flows.

Art. 9.o: Health, religion, ethnicity, biometrics, sexual life, union membership and similar data need an extra condition.
Art. 9.a: Mark special-category data on the data map and record the Article 9 condition you rely on.
Art. 9.e: They check each use of sensitive data has a valid condition.
Art. 9.r: Special data flag and condition on the data map.

Art. 10.o: Criminal convictions data can only be used under official authority or a legal permission.
Art. 10.a: If you run background checks, record the legal permission you rely on.
Art. 10.e: They ask what permits the checks.
Art. 10.r: Data map entry for vetting with its legal basis.

Art. 12.o: People can ask about their data. You have one month to answer, or three if it is complex and you told them.
Art. 12.a: Log every request in Requests. Watch the countdown and extend only with a reason.
Art. 12.e: They check response times and how you track them.

Art. 13.o: People must be told who you are, why you use their data, the lawful basis, who gets it, how long you keep it, and their rights.
Art. 13.a: Write a privacy notice for each group of people (customers, staff, website visitors) and record it under Notices and policies.
Art. 13.e: They read your notice against your data map.

Art. 15.o: People can ask for a copy of their data and information about how it is used.
Art. 15.a: Have a way to find all of one person's data across your systems, and log each access request.
Art. 15.e: They test whether you can find everything about one person.
Art. 15.r: Access requests in the tracker; search procedure.

Art. 16.o: People can ask you to fix data that is wrong or incomplete.
Art. 16.a: Log correction requests and update every system that holds the data.
Art. 16.e: They check the fix reached every copy.

Art. 17.o: The 'right to be forgotten'. Not absolute: you may need to keep some data by law.
Art. 17.a: Log erasure requests, delete what you can, and write down what you kept and why.
Art. 17.e: They check deletion happened, including in backups and with processors.

Art. 18.o: People can ask you to stop using their data for a while, for example while a dispute is checked.
Art. 18.a: Have a way to mark data as restricted and log these requests.
Art. 18.e: They ask how a restriction is applied in practice.

Art. 20.o: For data given by the person and used by consent or contract, they can ask for it in a common format.
Art. 20.a: Be able to export one person's data as a spreadsheet or similar file.
Art. 20.e: They check the format is usable.

Art. 21.o: People can object to some uses. An objection to direct marketing must always be honoured.
Art. 21.a: Keep a suppression list and log objections.
Art. 21.e: They check marketing stops after an objection.
Art. 21.r: Objection and stop-marketing requests in the tracker.

Art. 22.o: People have the right not to be judged only by an automated decision with big effects.
Art. 22.a: List automated decisions on the data map, offer a human review, and explain the logic.
Art. 22.e: They look for a way to challenge the decision.
Art. 22.r: Data map notes; DPIA for automated decisions.

Art. 24.o: The organisation is responsible for having fitting data protection policies.
Art. 24.a: Write and approve a data protection policy and the procedures below it.
Art. 24.e: They ask for your policy and who approved it.

Art. 25.o: New systems and projects should protect data by design, and collect the minimum by default.
Art. 25.a: Add a privacy check to every new project, and run a DPIA when it looks risky.
Art. 25.e: They ask how privacy is considered in projects.

Art. 26.o: When two organisations decide together how data is used, they must agree who does what.
Art. 26.a: Record joint controllers in Processors and suppliers and keep the arrangement on file.
Art. 26.r: Joint controller arrangement attached to the supplier record.

Art. 27.o: Organisations outside the EU that serve people in the EU usually need a representative there.
Art. 27.a: If this applies, appoint one and name them in your privacy notice.
Art. 27.e: They check the representative is named.

Art. 30.o: The 'data map'. A list of what personal data you use, why, and how.
Art. 30.a: Fill in the data map, give each entry an owner, and review it every year.
Art. 30.e: This is the core record a regulator will ask for.
Art. 30.r: The data map and its yearly reviews.

Art. 35.o: A DPIA (data protection impact assessment) is needed when processing is likely to be high risk.
Art. 35.a: Screen each data map entry. Where two or more risk signs apply, complete a DPIA.
Art. 35.e: They check high-risk processing has a DPIA done before it began.
Art. 35.r: DPIAs linked to data map entries.

Art. 36.o: If a DPIA shows high risk you cannot reduce, you must consult the regulator before starting.
Art. 36.a: Record the consultation on the DPIA.
Art. 36.e: They check you consulted where needed.

Art. 37.o: Public bodies, and organisations that monitor people on a large scale or handle lots of sensitive data, need a DPO.
Art. 37.a: Decide whether you need a DPO and write down why. If you do, appoint one and publish their contact details.
Art. 37.e: They check the decision and the DPO's independence.

Art. 39.o: Staff who handle personal data need to know the rules.
Art. 39.a: Give data protection training to staff and record who completed it.

Art. 32.o: Use security that fits the risk: access control, encryption, backups, testing.
Art. 32.a: Record the security measures for each data map entry and test them regularly.
Art. 32.e: They look at the measures and whether they match the risk.
Art. 32.r: Security notes on the data map; test results.

Art. 33.o: Unless a breach is unlikely to harm anyone, the regulator must be told within 72 hours of you becoming aware.
Art. 33.a: Log every breach in Breaches as soon as you know. Watch the countdown and record when you told the regulator.
Art. 33.e: They check the timeline from discovery to notice.
Art. 33.r: Breach log with times and references.

Art. 33(5).o: Every breach must be recorded, even ones you did not report, with your reasons.
Art. 33(5).a: Record the facts, effects, actions and your decision on every breach.
Art. 33(5).e: They ask for the full breach log.

Art. 34.o: If a breach is likely to cause high risk to people, they must be told without delay.
Art. 34.a: For each breach, decide whether to notify the people affected and write down why.
Art. 34.e: They check the decision and the message sent.
Art. 34.r: Breach log with decision; copy of the notice.

Art. 28.o: A processor handles data for you. You need a data processing agreement (DPA) with each one.
Art. 28.a: List every processor in Processors and suppliers, upload the signed DPA, and mark it Signed.
Art. 28.e: They ask for the contract with a named processor.
Art. 28.r: Signed DPAs attached to each processor.

Art. 28(2).o: Your processors may only use sub-processors you agreed to.
Art. 28(2).a: Keep your processors' sub-processor lists and record objections.
Art. 28(2).e: They check you were told about changes.
Art. 28(2).r: Sub-processor lists attached to supplier records.

Art. 44.o: Data may only leave the EU/EEA when it stays protected.
Art. 44.a: For each supplier, record if data leaves the EU, to which countries, and what covers it.
Art. 44.e: They ask how each transfer is covered.

Art. 46.o: Without an adequacy decision, transfers need safeguards such as standard contractual clauses (SCCs).
Art. 46.a: Sign SCCs or rely on another safeguard, and do a transfer risk assessment.
Art. 46.e: They ask for the clauses and the assessment.
Art. 46.r: SCCs and transfer risk assessments attached.
